Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 9 periods = 360 minutes
Total: 9 periods · 6h 0min

periods.activity_title: First Reading: Madhu and the Magical Banyan Tree

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us read (pp.88–92): read the story aloud, pausing at prediction prompts.

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces the story title and cover illustration. Students share what they think the story might be about, drawing on any familiar ideas about wishes or magic.

Let us read (pp.88–92) — teacher reads the narrative aloud expressively, pausing at the two in-text prompts ('What do you think Madhu will do now?' p.89; 'What do you think will happen now?' p.90) to invite quick oral predictions from pairs.
Students follow along for a second read of pp.88–90 as shared reading, taking turns reading a sentence each. Teacher supports decoding of food names such as kachori, jackfruit, and samosa.
Whole-class quick-share: students name one thing Madhu did that surprised them. Teacher notes key story moments on the board: wish, food, hiccups, water.

periods.teacher_notes: Madhu's character — a boy who loves food and makes a hasty wish — is the heart of this humorous narrative; keep the tone light and let students enjoy the comedy of the mounting food list. The food vocabulary (laddoos, matri, kachori, vada) is culturally rich; pronounce each item clearly and invite students to repeat. Unanchored prediction prompts are best handled orally here since no written response is expected at this stage.
materials: Blackboard or chart for key story moments

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us think — A (p.93): answer four questions about character and story events.

time_bands.activity: Teacher re-reads the passage on pp.91–92 (Madhu's hiccups and plea for water) aloud to refresh the whole story arc before discussion.

Let us think — A (p.93), questions 1 and 2: 'What did Madhu enjoy?' and 'Do you think the old man had magical powers? How do you know?' Students discuss in pairs, then share answers. Teacher models a complete-sentence response on the board.

Let us think — A (p.93), questions 3 and 4: 'Why did the tree ask Madhu to think over his wish?' and 'Name some things Madhu ate.' Students respond orally first, then write one sentence each in their notebooks.

Whole-class discussion: teacher draws out the story's theme — the value of water — by asking students how Madhu felt at the end. Key words (grateful, regret, important) are written on the board for reference.

periods.teacher_notes: Having read the story together, students can now revisit the logic of Madhu's wish and the tree's gentle warning; use question 3 to draw out the idea of thinking before acting. Students may give varied but valid answers for the old man's magical powers — accept evidence-based reasoning from the story text.

periods.activity_title: Think and Say: Hiccups, Water, and Wishes

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us think — B (p.93): guided conversation on hiccups, water, and personal wishes.

time_bands.activity: Teacher sets up the conversation: 'In the story, Madhu got hiccups and desperately wanted water. Let's talk about our own experiences.'

Let us think — B (p.93), questions 1 and 2: 'Have you experienced hiccups?' and 'What do you do when you get hiccups?' Students share in a circle. Teacher validates various home remedies and personal anecdotes.
Let us think — B (p.93), question 3: 'Do you think water is important? Why?' Students discuss in pairs and then report one reason to the class. Teacher lists reasons on the board.
Let us think — B (p.93), question 4: 'If you were in Madhu's place, what would you wish for and why?' Each student speaks one sentence aloud. Teacher encourages complete sentences and reasons.

periods.teacher_notes: This conversation flows naturally from Madhu's predicament — keep it personal and unhurried so every student has a turn. Question 4 invites imaginative thinking; accept any coherent wish with a reason, not just food-related ones.
materials: Blackboard for listing student reasons (water importance)

periods.activity_title: Listen and Retell: The Story Continues

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us listen — A (p.97): listen to two story passages and retell what happened next.

time_bands.activity: Teacher explains the listening activity: 'I will read two parts of the story. Listen carefully, then tell the class what happened next.'

Let us listen — A (p.97), part 1: teacher reads aloud 'Madhu said, Oh tree, let me have different types of food. Nothing else.' three to four times at a measured pace. Students listen with books closed.

Students respond orally: what happened after Madhu made his wish? Several volunteers retell the sequence (laddoos, fruits, savouries appearing). Teacher prompts with 'What came first? Then what?' to build sequencing.

Let us listen — A (p.97), part 2: teacher reads 'As he was eating, he suddenly got hiccups. He wanted water.' three to four times. Students listen, then retell what happened — the food everywhere, no water, the tree's reply.
Whole-class debrief: teacher asks one or two students to retell both parts together as a connected sequence. Class confirms the order using their books open at pp.91–92.

periods.teacher_notes: Listening retell works best when students cannot read along — keep books closed during the teacher's reading. The transcript at p.97 drives both listening passages; read each part slowly and repeat as specified in the NCF listening guidance for this stage.

periods.activity_title: Word Work: Food Baskets and Character Words

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us learn — A (p.94): classify food items into Fruits, Sweets, and Salty snacks baskets.
Let us learn — B & C (p.95): read character adjectives; fill in brave, polite, selfish, lazy.

time_bands.activity: Teacher revisits the long list of foods Madhu ate in the story and writes them on the board. Students read each word aloud together.

Let us learn — A (p.94): teacher draws three baskets (Fruits, Sweets, Salty snacks) on the board. Students take turns placing items from the Help Box (banana, kheer, melon, guava, kachori, potato chips, laddoo, vada, jackfruit, samosa) into the correct basket. Students write the completed table in their notebooks.

Let us learn — B (p.95): teacher reads the three model sentences about Madhu, the greedy man, and the generous old man. Class discusses what 'kind', 'greedy', and 'generous' mean by pointing to actions in the story.
Let us learn — C (p.95): students fill in the four blanks using brave, polite, selfish, lazy. Teacher reads each sentence, students choose the word in pairs, then confirm as a class.

periods.teacher_notes: The food-basket sort reinforces the story's vocabulary while building word categories — students who confuse kheer (sweet) with savoury items will need a reminder that kheer is a milk-based dessert. For the character adjectives, anchor each word to a story or real-life action so the meaning is concrete rather than abstract.

periods.activity_title: Word Work: Joining Sentences with 'and' and 'but'

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us learn — D (pp.96–97): rewrite five sentence pairs using 'and' or 'but'.

homework.task_brief: Fun with Words — B & C (p.99): identify the shared first letter in alliterative pyramids; write your own.

time_bands.activity: Teacher writes two short sentences on the board drawn from the story context: 'Madhu sat under the tree. He ate his lunch.' and models joining them with 'and'. Then writes 'Madhu wanted water. The tree had given only food.' and models joining with 'but'.
Let us learn — D (pp.96–97): teacher reads the two model examples from the textbook with students. Class discusses: when do we use 'and' (adding similar ideas) and when 'but' (showing contrast)?
Students work through sentences 1–5 (pp.96–97) in pairs, writing the combined sentence in their notebooks. Teacher circulates and checks that 'and' joins like actions and 'but' signals contrast.

Whole-class sharing: volunteers read their combined sentences aloud. Teacher highlights any errors gently — particularly sentence 4 where 'but' signals Dolma's conflict — and confirms correct forms on the board.

periods.teacher_notes: Students commonly apply 'and' everywhere; sentence 2 (cartoons vs movies) and sentences 4–5 require 'but' because the second clause contradicts the first. Using story examples (Madhu wished for food, but he forgot water) keeps the grammar grounded in familiar context. The alliterative-pyramid homework is creative and independent, requiring no earlier class activity.

periods.activity_title: Writing: Sentence Completion — Why Madhu Did What He Did

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us write — A (p.100): complete four sentences about Madhu's actions with reasons.

time_bands.activity: Teacher writes the four sentence starters on the board (p.100). Class reads them together. Teacher models completing the first one orally: 'Madhu shared his food with the old man because the old man was hungry and Madhu was kind.'

Students discuss sentences 2 and 3 with a partner — 'Madhu was happy because…' and 'After eating fruits, Madhu asked for savouries because…' — drawing on the story. Teacher prompts: 'Go back to the story. What does the text tell us?'
Students write all four completed sentences in their notebooks independently. Teacher circulates, checking that each completion is rooted in the story and forms a complete sentence.

Peer-share: students swap notebooks and read each other's sentence 4 ('Madhu asked for water because…'). They check that the reason makes sense and the sentence is complete. A few pairs share with the class.

periods.teacher_notes: Having explored the story's events through reading and discussion, students can draw directly on Madhu's motivations to complete these prompts — encourage them to use evidence from the text rather than guessing. Watch for sentence 3: students may say 'because he was greedy' (acceptable) but those who can name specific fruits he ate before asking for savouries demonstrate stronger story recall.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us write — A (p.98): continue the story of Vijaya, a girl in a small village.

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads the story starter aloud: 'Vijaya is a young girl. She lives with her father, mother, grandmother and grandfather in a small village. Each day…' Teacher and class brainstorm on the board: what might Vijaya do each day?
Teacher models writing two sentences aloud, thinking through choices ('Does Vijaya go to school? Does she help at home?'). The modelled sentences are left on the board as a scaffold.

Students write their story continuation in their notebooks. Teacher encourages 3–5 sentences, reminding them to include at least one event and one feeling. Teacher circulates and offers individual support with vocabulary and sentence structure.
Three or four volunteers read their story aloud. Class listens and shares one thing they liked. Teacher gives brief oral feedback on ideas and sentence completeness.

periods.teacher_notes: The Vijaya prompt is open-ended; students may draw on daily life in any setting — village, town, or their own home — since the story's theme of family and everyday life is the bridge. Encourage variety: a student who writes about cooking with grandmother and another who writes about fetching water are both valid and thematically resonant with the chapter's message about simple daily necessities.
materials: Blackboard for brainstorm and model sentences

periods.activity_title: Hands-On: Making a Fruit and Vegetable Table Mat

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us do (pp.100–101): make a fruit/vegetable table mat using torn coloured paper and A4 sheet.

time_bands.activity: Teacher displays the six step-by-step illustrations in the textbook (p.101) and reads the instructions aloud. Students lay out their materials on the desk: A4 sheet, coloured paper, glue, pencil or sketch pen.
Step 1 and 2 (p.101): students draw the outline of one or two fruits or vegetables of their choice on the A4 sheet, then tear their coloured paper into small pieces.

Steps 3 and 4 (p.101): students paste the torn coloured paper pieces inside the fruit outlines, filling each shape with an appropriate colour. Teacher circulates, encouraging students to work carefully and cover the whole outline.
Students write the name of each fruit or vegetable they drew as a label on their mat, using the story's food vocabulary as a reference list on the board.

Gallery walk: students place their finished mats on their desks. Class does a quick walk to see each other's work. Teacher closes by connecting the craft to the story: 'Madhu wished for all these fruits — now we have made them ourselves!'

periods.teacher_notes: All materials for this craft — A4 paper, coloured paper, glue — must be brought in or provided at the start of this unit; nothing depends on a previous sitting. Labelling each fruit links the craft activity back to the word-category knowledge from the food-basket sort, reinforcing the story's food vocabulary in a hands-on way.
materials: Optional: clear plastic sheet for covering

items.item_stem: What did the magical banyan tree give Madhu first after he made his wish for food?

what_each_option_reveals.C: Students who choose this may recall that water was central to the story but confuse the resolution with the initial wish fulfilment.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Suggests the student remembers the savouries list but has not tracked the sequence — laddoos came before savouries.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Reveals the student associates kheer with the story (Madhu tried it for hiccups) but has confused the order of events.

items.item_stem: Your teacher will read this aloud: 'As Madhu was eating, he suddenly got hiccups. He wanted water. He looked around — there was food everywhere but no water.' Listen carefully. Is the following statement true or false? 'Madhu could not get water because the banyan tree refused to speak to him.'

options.text: Madhu could not get water because the banyan tree refused to speak to him.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: False. Madhu could not get water because he had wished only for food, not water, and the tree could only grant what he had wished for.
